opus-5.5.text:
I think it's almost an inevitable direction. If you look back at the last few years, the biggest successes, especially large language models, came from learning on text. Text is incredibly powerful because it's a compressed representation of human knowledge. But it's also a very thin slice of reality. Language is something humans invented to describe the world. It's not the world itself.

So the models we have today are very good at manipulating symbols, at reasoning in language, at writing code. But if you ask whether they really understand how a cup falls off a table, how objects persist when you look away, how a room is laid out in 3D, or what happens when you push something, that understanding is still very shallow. A four-year-old has a better intuitive physics model than our best systems.

To me, a world model means a system that can build an internal representation of the environment, predict how that environment will evolve, and reason about what happens if it takes certain actions. That's what intelligence in animals and humans is grounded in. We perceive, we form a model, we plan, we act, and we update. Language comes on top of that, not underneath it.

There are also practical reasons. If you want AI to work in the physical world, in robotics, autonomous driving, embodied agents, or even scientific discovery, you can't rely only on text. You need spatial understanding and an understanding of dynamics and causality. And the text data on the internet is running out in some sense, while visual and sensory data from the real world is essentially unlimited.

So I see the field moving from "models that talk about the world" to "models that actually model the world." Vision is a big part of that, which is why I care so much about it. For a long time, vision research was seen as a supporting role for language models, like giving them a pair of eyes. I think it should be the other way around: visual and spatial intelligence is the foundation, and language is one interface on top of it.

That said, I don't think anyone has the full answer yet. Whether it's video generation, latent predictive models, 3D representations, or something else, we're still in an exploratory phase. But the direction feels very clear to me, and that's why it's such an exciting time to be working on this.

r001.rationale: It says current language models manipulate symbols well but have shallow understanding of physical reality, motivating a move toward systems that model the world.

r002.rationale: It discusses language reasoning and planning generally, but does not mention chain-of-thought or compare it with MPC-level planning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's not so much that researchers decided to go toward world models as a slogan; it's that we've been running into the same wall from several directions at once, and "world model" is just the name for what's on the other side of that wall.

Let me explain what I mean. If you look at the last few years, the dominant recipe has been: take an enormous amount of data, usually text, and train a model to predict the next token. That worked astonishingly well, better than most of us expected. But if you spend time actually working with these systems, you notice there's a kind of ceiling that's hard to articulate. The model knows a lot of things, but it doesn't really understand how things happen. It has read about the world, but it hasn't lived in it. Language is a compressed, lossy summary that humans wrote for other humans who already share a body, a physical environment, a sense of time and causality. The model gets the summary without the thing being summarized.

So when people say we're moving toward world models, what they really mean is we're trying to give the system that missing part: an internal representation of how the world evolves. If I do this, what happens next? If this object is here and I look away, is it still there? What's behind the door? These sound trivial, but they're the foundation of almost everything we call intelligence, and current models are weirdly fragile on them.

From the vision side, which is where I come from, the push has been very natural. For a long time, vision was treated as a recognition problem: here's an image, tell me what's in it. But recognition isn't really the point of vision in animals. Vision exists so you can act. You need to understand space, you need to understand what will change and what won't, you need to be able to imagine the consequences of movement. So once you take vision seriously as a route to intelligence rather than a labeling task, you end up asking for a world model almost by definition.

And then from the robotics and agents side, there's a very practical pressure. If you want a system to do things in the real world, you cannot afford to learn purely by trial and error in reality. It's too slow, too expensive, sometimes dangerous. So you want the model to be able to simulate internally, to plan in imagination, and that requires a learned model of dynamics. That's an old idea, honestly, going back decades in reinforcement learning, but now the representation learning is good enough that it feels achievable rather than aspirational.

There's also something about scale. We've had this bet that scaling data and compute gets you most of the way, and I partly believe it. But the data that encodes how the world works is not text. It's video, it's interaction, it's embodied experience. There's vastly more of it than text, and we've barely touched it. So even from a purely pragmatic "where's the next big source of signal" point of view, the answer points toward learning from the world directly.

I'd add one caveat, because I think the term gets used loosely. A world model isn't just a video generator that produces pretty frames. Generating plausible pixels and actually understanding the underlying structure are different things, and I think the field sometimes conflates them. The interesting question for me is whether we can learn representations that capture what matters, the state, the causality, the persistence, without having to reconstruct every detail. That's where I think the real research is, and where I'm not sure yet what the right answer looks like.

So to summarize: it's convergence. Language models hit the limits of what text can teach. Vision matured past recognition. Robotics needs imagination. And the biggest untapped data is the world itself. All of those roads lead to the same place, so naturally the field is walking there.

r001.rationale: The response says language models trained on text know facts but lack an internal understanding of how the world evolves, calling them fragile on basic physical questions. It presents that limitation as a reason to move toward world models.

r002.rationale: The response discusses planning in imagination for robotics, but does not mention chain-of-thought or compare it with MPC-level planning.

astra-6.text:
I think it comes from a basic limitation of learning from static observations. You can train a model to recognize what is in an image, or predict the next word, and it can become very capable. But if you want it to act in the world, it also needs some understanding of how things change: if I take this action, what happens next?

That’s the motivation for a world model. It doesn’t necessarily mean building a perfect simulator of everything. It means learning enough about the environment to predict the consequences of actions and use those predictions to make decisions.

For example, recognizing a cup is one problem. Knowing what will happen if you push it toward the edge of a table is another. That involves motion, physical constraints, and uncertainty. And if a robot wants to pick up that cup, its understanding has to be useful for control.

So I see the movement as a gradual expansion from recognition to prediction, and from prediction to action. These capabilities overlap; it’s not that one research direction suddenly replaces another. But as we ask AI systems to do more than answer questions—to interact, plan, and adapt—the need for some kind of world model becomes much clearer.

r001.rationale: The response mentions next-word prediction and the need to predict action consequences, but does not present language models’ rudimentary world-model behavior as a reason for the shift.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss chain-of-thought reasoning or compare it with MPC-level planning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a natural progression. If we want AI to do more than recognize patterns—if we want it to act, plan, and solve problems—it needs some understanding of how the world changes. What happens if I take this action? What might happen next? And can I predict that without having to try everything in the real world?

Language gives us a very powerful starting point because it contains so much human knowledge. But a description of the world isn’t the whole world. There’s motion, geometry, physical interaction, and a lot of things that are difficult to express in words. So moving toward learning from video and interaction makes sense.

But I wouldn’t say there’s one agreed-upon definition of a world model, or that we already know the right path. Predicting what an image will look like next is one thing; learning a representation that actually helps you make decisions is another. To me, that’s the interesting question: can the model learn enough about how the world works to use that knowledge in a new situation?
